transcript.content: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess it’s this memorial I’m putting together for my brother. It started out simple, you know, just a few songs and maybe some pictures, but then I got to thinking about the old places we used to go, and who should be invited, and the displays, and now I’m on the phone most days tracking people down and planning trips and all that.

My wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been showing up for the walking group much either. She says I’ve pushed everything else aside for it. I don’t know, it just feels important, but it’s gotten bigger than I meant it to.
While you’ve been working on the memorial, have you felt unusually upbeat or energized compared with your normal self?

Yeah… I suppose I have. Some days I feel sort of lit up, like I’ve got this purpose, like if I get it all right then the whole town will finally understand what our family was about.

But then if my wife says I’m overdoing it, or someone at the senior center starts questioning where the display should go, I get sharp with them. I don’t mean to, but I snap, like they’re getting in the way of something important.
Have you been needing less sleep than usual?

I don’t know if I’d say I “need” less sleep. I mean, some nights I’m up later because I start thinking about who still needs calling, or I remember a box of photos in the closet—funny, my brother had this old fishing picture everyone used to laugh about—and then I’m looking for it and the evening gets away from me.

But whether I’m actually sleeping less than usual… I’m not sure. I haven’t really been keeping track.
Have other people told you that you’ve been talking faster than usual lately?

Yes, my pastor has said something like that. At the senior center meetings, I start explaining how the songs fit with the quilts and the photos, and then one thing reminds me of another—like the hymn my brother liked, though honestly he’d only admit it after a couple coffees—and before I know it, I’ve talked right over three people.

My pastor will sort of put his hand up gentle and say, “Aaron, let’s let someone else speak.” So… yes, I guess people have noticed I’m going on too fast or too much.
Have you felt that you have a special ability or unique responsibility to make this memorial matter more than anyone else could?

I don’t know that I’d put it like that… “special ability” sounds awfully grand. I just—well, I’ve been around long enough to remember how my mother set tables for half the neighborhood, and how my brother used to fix people’s porch steps without taking a dime, and those things get lost if somebody doesn’t put them in the right order.

Now, whether that means I’m the only one who can do it… I don’t know. My wife says other people can help, and she’s probably right. It just feels like I know the pieces, you know? Like that picture from the church picnic—half the folks in it are gone now, and if I don’t say who they are, then who’s going to?
Have you been more active than usual in planning or doing things lately?

Yes… I suppose I have. That’s kind of what brought me in, really. This memorial for my brother started as a little thing, you know, maybe a few songs and some pictures, and now I’m spending most days chasing down hymns, calling people, figuring out displays, even thinking about trips to pick up things or talk to folks.

And I mean, it all feels important—my brother was the kind of man who’d show up with a toolbox before you even asked—but my wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been to the walking group much, and just about everything else has gotten pushed aside. So yes, I’ve been doing a lot more than usual, I guess.
How long have you been feeling this unusually energized and driven?

About two months, I’d say. It really started after my brother passed and I began working on his tribute. At first it was just, you know, picking a song or two, maybe sorting some photos, but then I kept seeing more that ought to be included—people he helped, stories from church, little things like that.

So… yes, roughly two months I’ve been feeling this driven about it.
Before your brother died, had you ever had another period when you felt unusually energized and driven like this?

Well… before he died? I’m trying to think. I’ve always been a person who gets involved in things—church suppers, fixing up the house, helping my wife with odds and ends—but this particular push, this kind of being pulled along by it, has really been these last couple months.

It started after my brother passed and I began putting together the tribute for him. Before that, I don’t know that I’d say it was like this. This has been going on about two months, tied up with the memorial.
During this time, have you felt more important or more capable than usual?

More important? I don’t know… I haven’t really thought of it that way. I mean, I do feel like this memorial needs to be done right, but that’s because he was my brother, you know? He helped a lot of people.

Capable… well, I’ve been making calls and arranging things, but I wouldn’t say I suddenly feel like some big important man. Though my wife did say I was acting like I was running the whole church committee, and that reminds me, Mrs. Hanley used to run those bake sales like a general—she could get forty pies donated by Thursday without raising her voice.

So… I’m not sure. I feel responsible for it, I guess, more than important.
Aside from working on your brother’s memorial, have you been taking on other new projects or activities more than usual?

Well, not so much new projects besides the memorial, I guess. It’s more that the memorial itself keeps turning into ten different projects. I start with one song, then I’m calling someone about photos, then I’m planning a display, then I think maybe I should drive over and talk to somebody who knew him from church years back.

Most days I’m wrapped up in that—songs, calls, displays, little trips—and my wife says I’ve let the garden go, and I haven’t been keeping up with the walking group either. She says I’ve pushed almost everything else aside for this.
During these past two months, have you actually felt unusually happy or euphoric?

Happy? I don’t know if I’d call it happy exactly. There are moments I feel… lit up, I guess. Like I’ve got this purpose, like if I get the memorial just right, the whole town will finally understand who my brother was, who our family is.

But then it turns quick. If my wife says maybe the display is too much, or someone at the senior center tells me to slow down, I get sharp with them. I snap before I even think. So it’s not just happy—it’s more like I’m charged up, and people keep getting in the way.
Since your brother died, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

I don’t know… two weeks is hard to measure. Since he died, I’ve had low moments, sure. I miss him, and some mornings I sit there thinking about things we should’ve said.

But most of the time I’ve been busy with the memorial, and that sort of carries me along. My wife would probably tell you I don’t sit still long enough to be down. Though after my father passed, I remember my mother wore black for nearly a year—different times, you know, people didn’t talk about feelings the way they do now.

So… depressed most of the day, nearly every day? I’m not sure I’d say that. I’ve been upset, yes, but I don’t know about like that.
During this time, have you had more energy than usual nearly every day?

Yes… yes, I suppose I have. I don’t sit in my chair the way I used to, that’s for sure. I’ll tell myself I’m just going to sort one little box, and next thing I’m hauling things from the closet, stacking papers on the table, making three phone calls, walking back and forth from the kitchen to the den like I forgot what room I belong in.

It’s funny, my father used to say a man slows down after a certain age, but lately I feel like there’s more steam in me than there ought to be. Not young exactly, but like my body keeps pushing me up again every time I try to settle.
During this time, have you been sleeping much less than usual and still felt rested?

Sleep… I don’t know. I mean, at my age sleep gets funny anyway, doesn’t it? My mother used to wake up before dawn every day and say that was just how the house told you it was morning.

I’ve had some nights where I’m up earlier, or I don’t stay asleep the way I used to, but whether I’m “rested”… that’s harder to say. Sometimes I get moving because there’s something to do, not because I woke up feeling like I had a full night. I haven’t really kept track of the hours.
During this time, have your thoughts been racing?

Yes… they do jump around on me. I’ll start thinking, “I should make a proper display case,” you know, something nice, and before I’ve even finished that thought I’m thinking maybe I ought to drive out and find that cousin we lost touch with, and then some old ballad lyric pops in my head—my brother used to hum one, or maybe it was my uncle, I can’t remember.

And then I try to write it all down so it makes sense, but it’s like the thoughts won’t line up. They keep cutting ahead of each other. I wouldn’t say I’m trying to think fast, it just… happens that way.
Has this memorial planning caused serious problems in your day-to-day life?

Yes… I suppose it has, though I hate calling it “serious,” because that makes it sound like I’m doing something wrong.

But I’ve missed my walking group a few times, and the book club too. I used to like sitting there and hearing what everyone thought, even if half of them never finished the book. And the garden—oh, my tomatoes would be ashamed of me this year. I keep meaning to get out there, but then I see something that should go in the memorial display, or I think of someone I need to call, and the whole day turns.

People at the senior center have gotten upset with me. They say I keep bringing everything back to the memorial, and maybe I do. My wife says our days are all about calming me down or stopping me from making another call, taking another trip, starting another argument. I don’t mean for it to be that way, but it’s like everything else gets pushed to the side.
During these past two months, have you been more distractible than usual?

Distractible… I’m not sure how to measure that. I’ve always been the sort who notices little things—the kettle making that high sound, a bird at the window, a bit of dust on a picture frame—and then I remember something my father used to say about keeping a house presentable.

But these past couple months… I don’t know. My wife might say I don’t stay on one thing, but sometimes I think that’s just because there are a lot of things needing attention. I’ll start to answer a letter, then see a clipping, then think I should put it somewhere safe. Is that distractible? I’m not sure.
During these past two months, have you felt more self-confident than usual?

More self-confident… I’m not sure I’d call it that. I mean, some days I feel very certain about what ought to be done, but confidence is a funny word, isn’t it? My father used to say confidence was just knowing how to stand straight in church even when your shoes hurt.

I haven’t really thought, “Oh, I’m better than everyone,” if that’s what you mean. I just… I don’t know. I’ve been more set on certain things, maybe. But self-confident? I’d have to think about that.
During these past two months, have you felt unusually irritable most of the day nearly every day?

Yes… irritable, I suppose that’s fair. Not all the time exactly, but it comes on strong. I’ll feel sort of lit up, like I’ve finally got the purpose of this memorial clear in my head and the whole town is going to understand what our family meant, what my father stood for—he had this way of polishing his shoes before every parade, you know, even if it rained.

And then if my wife says, “Maybe wait before calling them,” or someone at the senior center questions where the display should go, I snap. I don’t mean to. It’s just… they feel like they’re slowing down something important. Then afterward I know I sounded sharp. But in the moment, yes, I get very irritated.
During this time, have you heard or seen things that other people said were not there?

Well… yes, I suppose so, though it sounds strange saying it that way.

Sometimes when I’m at the kitchen table sorting through my brother’s old song sheets—you know, he always kept them folded wrong, drove my mother crazy—I hear him behind me, clear as anything. Humming, mostly. Or saying which tune comes next.

But when I turn around, there’s no one there, and my wife says she didn’t hear anything at all. So… yes, I guess that counts.

patient.answer:
Happy? I don’t know if I’d call it happy exactly. There are moments I feel… lit up, I guess. Like I’ve got this purpose, like if I get the memorial just right, the whole town will finally understand who my brother was, who our family is.

But then it turns quick. If my wife says maybe the display is too much, or someone at the senior center tells me to slow down, I get sharp with them. I snap before I even think. So it’s not just happy—it’s more like I’m charged up, and people keep getting in the way.

inference.note: Symptoms are clearly tied to a bereavement-related stressor with mixed anxiety/behavioral disturbance features, so F43.23 is added and F43.21/F42 are less supported. Bipolar spectrum remains possible because of 2 months of increased energy, pressured speech, irritability, and overinvolvement, but classic euphoric/grandiose features remain limited and symptoms are stress-linked.

doctor.intent: Assess whether there has been a major depressive episode, which would help distinguish adjustment disorder from bipolar disorder or unipolar depression.
doctor.question: Since your brother died, have you had a period of at least two weeks when you felt depressed or down most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a depressive episode or persistent depressed mood for at least two weeks, but the provided symptom profile does not include a depression-related symptom item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know… two weeks is hard to measure. Since he died, I’ve had low moments, sure. I miss him, and some mornings I sit there thinking about things we should’ve said.

But most of the time I’ve been busy with the memorial, and that sort of carries me along. My wife would probably tell you I don’t sit still long enough to be down. Though after my father passed, I remember my mother wore black for nearly a year—different times, you know, people didn’t talk about feelings the way they do now.

So… depressed most of the day, nearly every day? I’m not sure I’d say that. I’ve been upset, yes, but I don’t know about like that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a discrete period of abnormally increased goal-directed activity or energy nearly every day, which is essential for distinguishing bipolar hypomania/mania from an adjustment reaction or uncomplicated depression.
doctor.question: During this time, have you had more energy than usual nearly every day?

target_item.name: Increased_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I can’t seem to sit in my chair like I used to; I’m up hauling boxes, making calls, rearranging papers, walking room to room, feeling like my body has more steam in it than a man my age ought to have.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether I have had more energy than usual nearly every day during this period.

patient.answer:
Yes… yes, I suppose I have. I don’t sit in my chair the way I used to, that’s for sure. I’ll tell myself I’m just going to sort one little box, and next thing I’m hauling things from the closet, stacking papers on the table, making three phone calls, walking back and forth from the kitchen to the den like I forgot what room I belong in.

It’s funny, my father used to say a man slows down after a certain age, but lately I feel like there’s more steam in me than there ought to be. Not young exactly, but like my body keeps pushing me up again every time I try to settle.

inference.note: F32.9 is less likely because he does not endorse a clear ≥2-week period of depressed mood most of the day nearly every day; current picture remains stressor-linked with elevated/irritable activation and increased energy after bereavement, so adjustment disorder vs bipolar spectrum remain the leading considerations.

doctor.intent: Determine whether his increased energy and activity have caused a clear decrease in sleep need, which would help distinguish a hypomanic/manic episode from an adjustment disorder related to bereavement.
doctor.question: During this time, have you been sleeping much less than usual and still felt rested?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about decreased need for sleep, but the provided symptom profile does not include a sleep-related item.

patient.answer:
Sleep… I don’t know. I mean, at my age sleep gets funny anyway, doesn’t it? My mother used to wake up before dawn every day and say that was just how the house told you it was morning.

I’ve had some nights where I’m up earlier, or I don’t stay asleep the way I used to, but whether I’m “rested”… that’s harder to say. Sometimes I get moving because there’s something to do, not because I woke up feeling like I had a full night. I haven’t really kept track of the hours.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the increased energy and pressured behavior are accompanied by a core manic symptom of racing thoughts, which would help distinguish a bipolar spectrum episode from an adjustment reaction to bereavement.
doctor.question: During this time, have your thoughts been racing?

target_item.name: Racing_Thoughts
target_item.manifestation: My mind keeps jumping from one idea to the next—one minute it’s a display case, then a road trip to find a cousin, then a verse from a ballad—and I can’t slow it down enough to write it in order.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question directly asks whether my thoughts have been racing during this time.

patient.answer:
Yes… they do jump around on me. I’ll start thinking, “I should make a proper display case,” you know, something nice, and before I’ve even finished that thought I’m thinking maybe I ought to drive out and find that cousin we lost touch with, and then some old ballad lyric pops in my head—my brother used to hum one, or maybe it was my uncle, I can’t remember.

And then I try to write it all down so it makes sense, but it’s like the thoughts won’t line up. They keep cutting ahead of each other. I wouldn’t say I’m trying to think fast, it just… happens that way.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the increased energy and activity have caused a clear functional impairment severe enough to support a manic episode rather than an adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: Has this memorial planning caused serious problems in your day-to-day life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’ve missed my walking group and book club, let the garden go, and upset friends at the senior center because everything has become about the memorial display. My wife says our days revolve around calming me down or redirecting me from another call, trip, or argument.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the memorial planning has caused serious problems in day-to-day life, which directly matches functional impairment: missing usual activities, neglecting the garden, upsetting friends, and disrupting life with his wife.

patient.answer:
Yes… I suppose it has, though I hate calling it “serious,” because that makes it sound like I’m doing something wrong.

But I’ve missed my walking group a few times, and the book club too. I used to like sitting there and hearing what everyone thought, even if half of them never finished the book. And the garden—oh, my tomatoes would be ashamed of me this year. I keep meaning to get out there, but then I see something that should go in the memorial display, or I think of someone I need to call, and the whole day turns.

People at the senior center have gotten upset with me. They say I keep bringing everything back to the memorial, and maybe I do. My wife says our days are all about calming me down or stopping me from making another call, taking another trip, starting another argument. I don’t mean for it to be that way, but it’s like everything else gets pushed to the side.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the increased energy and overinvolvement are accompanied by a core manic sign independent of bereavement-related stress, helping distinguish bipolar disorder from an adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During these past two months, have you been more distractible than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about distractibility during the past two months, but the provided symptom profile does not include a distractibility item. Racing thoughts and increased activity are related manic symptoms, but they are not the same as distractibility.

patient.answer:
Distractible… I’m not sure how to measure that. I’ve always been the sort who notices little things—the kettle making that high sound, a bird at the window, a bit of dust on a picture frame—and then I remember something my father used to say about keeping a house presentable.

But these past couple months… I don’t know. My wife might say I don’t stay on one thing, but sometimes I think that’s just because there are a lot of things needing attention. I’ll start to answer a letter, then see a clipping, then think I should put it somewhere safe. Is that distractible? I’m not sure.

doctor.intent: Clarify whether the elevated/activated state includes a hallmark manic symptom independent of grief-related busyness by assessing increase in self-confidence/grandiosity.
doctor.question: During these past two months, have you felt more self-confident than usual?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about increased self-confidence or grandiosity, but the provided symptom profile does not include a specific item for that symptom.

patient.answer:
More self-confident… I’m not sure I’d call it that. I mean, some days I feel very certain about what ought to be done, but confidence is a funny word, isn’t it? My father used to say confidence was just knowing how to stand straight in church even when your shoes hurt.

I haven’t really thought, “Oh, I’m better than everyone,” if that’s what you mean. I just… I don’t know. I’ve been more set on certain things, maybe. But self-confident? I’d have to think about that.

doctor.intent: Determine whether there has been a clear period of abnormally elevated or irritable mood outside normal grief, which would support a manic/hypomanic episode over an adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During these past two months, have you felt unusually irritable most of the day nearly every day?

target_item.name: Elevated_Irritable_Mood
target_item.manifestation: I’ll feel lit up and full of purpose one minute, like the whole town is finally going to understand our family, and then I snap at my wife or someone at the senior center if they slow me down or question the display.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking specifically about unusually irritable mood over the past two months, which directly matches the Elevated_Irritable_Mood symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yes… irritable, I suppose that’s fair. Not all the time exactly, but it comes on strong. I’ll feel sort of lit up, like I’ve finally got the purpose of this memorial clear in my head and the whole town is going to understand what our family meant, what my father stood for—he had this way of polishing his shoes before every parade, you know, even if it rained.

And then if my wife says, “Maybe wait before calling them,” or someone at the senior center questions where the display should go, I snap. I don’t mean to. It’s just… they feel like they’re slowing down something important. Then afterward I know I sounded sharp. But in the moment, yes, I get very irritated.

doctor.intent: Determine whether he has had psychotic symptoms, which would strongly favor bipolar I disorder over adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: During this time, have you heard or seen things that other people said were not there?

target_item.name: Hallucinations
target_item.manifestation: Sometimes when I’m sorting his song sheets at the kitchen table, I hear my brother’s voice clear as day humming behind me or telling me which tune comes next, even though nobody else in the house hears a thing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about hearing or seeing things that others say are not there, which directly refers to hallucinations.

patient.answer:
Well… yes, I suppose so, though it sounds strange saying it that way.

Sometimes when I’m at the kitchen table sorting through my brother’s old song sheets—you know, he always kept them folded wrong, drove my mother crazy—I hear him behind me, clear as anything. Humming, mostly. Or saying which tune comes next.

But when I turn around, there’s no one there, and my wife says she didn’t hear anything at all. So… yes, I guess that counts.

inference.note: Psychotic symptoms (hearing his deceased brother) during a 2-month period of elevated/irritable mood, increased energy, pressured speech, racing thoughts, and impairment raise bipolar disorder to a manic episode with psychotic features (F31.2) rather than unspecified bipolar (F31.9). Adjustment disorder candidates remain because symptoms are clearly triggered by bereavement, though psychosis/manic syndrome makes them less likely.

opening_question.intent: Learn the patient's main reason for seeking psychiatric care today
opening_question.question: Hello, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a distinct approximately 2-month period of elevated/energized and irritable mood with increased goal-directed activity, pressured/excessive speech, racing thoughts, and significant functional impairment centered on an expansive memorial project. He also reports hearing his deceased brother's voice/humming when no one is present, indicating psychotic symptoms. This symptom cluster exceeds an adjustment reaction to bereavement and is most consistent with a manic episode with psychotic symptoms in bipolar affective disorder.
